implementation_notes: Crow supplies dispatch and response construction, not the ADR split: CROW_ROUTE(app, "/users/<int>") registers exactly one lambda per route (optionally taking const crow::request&), the lambda is the Action, and the returned crow::response - or a crow::json::wvalue the framework serialises - is the Responder. The Domain stays a plain function or class that never sees crow::request, which is what keeps it testable and reusable. The separate responder object is worth writing when one action must answer in several formats; otherwise returning the response directly is the idiomatic form.
pitfalls: Handlers run on Crow's thread pool: touching shared domain state without synchronisation is a data race.
A response is strictly tied to its route - returning a reference to a local or a type the route cannot convert fails to compile or dangles.
Route registration happens before run(), so lambdas that capture locals by reference outlive the scope that registered them.

variants.name: Drogon handler with HttpRequestPtr / HttpResponsePtr callback
variants.idiom_name: Drogon handler method / registerHandler with HttpResponsePtr callback
variants.implementation_notes: Drogon inverts the shape: a handler is a member function or a lambda registered with registerHandler that receives const HttpRequestPtr& plus a std::function<void(const HttpResponsePtr&)> callback, and it must deliver the response by invoking callback(resp). The Responder role is the code that builds the HttpResponsePtr - HttpResponse::newHttpResponse(), newHttpJsonResponse(), newFileResponse(), newRedirectResponse() - so the response object is explicit and shared, which suits large applications that already have Drogon controllers and filters. Drogon requires C++17 (optionally C++20 with Boost), a higher floor than the Crow variant.
pitfalls: Forgetting to call callback(resp) leaves the request hanging until the client times out; every path through the handler must deliver exactly one response.
Handlers execute on HTTP server threads and must not block on synchronous I/O or long domain work, or the server's throughput collapses.
Response objects are shared_ptr: mutating one after handing it to the callback races with the framework sending it.
